utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to inform the parties that the Chamber has considered whether any follow-up should be given at this moment in relation to Mr. van Rooyen. The Chamber, as matters stand now, does not intend to give it a follow-up in this courtroom. Therefore, Mr. Waespi, you're free to discuss the matter with Mr. van Rooyen, and, as you said, you would report back, the Chamber appreciates that it will be informed about the outcome. Then we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. We will turn in private session again for one second for ... and even we have to turn into closed session. The parties may understand why. We still have to wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Closed session for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mrksic, I'd like to address a few matters before the -- Mr. Misetic will have an opportunity to examine you as a witness. First of all, everyone, if called as a witness, is under a duty to testify. The Chamber is aware that you would not be inclined to appear as a witness but that you waited until you received a subpoena. That subpoena has been issued. I inform you that Rule 77, under (A)(i) specifically states that you can be held in contempt if you, as a witness before a Chamber, contumaciously refuse or fails to answer questions. That means you have to answer questions that are put to you. That's your duty as a witness, and if you would fail to do so, contempt proceedings could be initiated against you and failing to answer is punishable. And the maximum penalty for contempt of court including failing to answer questions is - and I have to look at it - I think a maximum term of imprisonment of 7 years, or a fine not exceeding 100.000 Euros or both these penalties, that are the maximum penalties if someone commits contempt of court, and that includes failing to answer questions. At the same time, I would like to inform you, that if you are asked questions and where you think that your answer might tend to incriminate yourself, that you may object to answering such a question. The Chamber will then consider the matter, and we can either decide that you don't have to answer the question, but we also can compel you to answer the question. And testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against you for any offence, apart from giving false testimony. So if you answer the question, if it is not truthful, then, of course, that would be -- that would be an offence in itself. But apart from that exception that evidence cannot be held against you. I also inform you that this is, of course, specifically focussing on Tribunal proceedings. It has never happened, to my knowledge, that it was used in any other court. The Chamber inquired whether there's any intention to prosecute you anywhere else. The Chamber is aware that you still have to serve quite a lot of time in detention, because you have been finally convicted and sentenced and are awaiting transfer to a country where you will serve your sentence. So, at this moment, there is no indication that a risk of being prosecuted elsewhere exists. Finally, I address the following matter. The Chamber was informed that you were hesitant/not inclined to testify because your lawyer would not be present. The Chamber has considered this, and came to the following provisional conclusions. You are aware already of some time that there was an intention to call you as a witness. From the communications between these parties and the Chamber, the Chamber is aware that - is there any problem in -- the Chamber is aware that those who have assisted you as counsel in the proceedings against yourself as an accused were informed about all these steps preparing for your testimony in court. Nevertheless no steps were taken for any counsel to be present here, although they were aware of -- and they have not in any way communicated with the Chamber any concerns. From what we understand the only thing that was done is that it was communicated to the Prosecution that you would prefer not to testify if counsel were not present. Now, there is no right to be assisted by counsel if you appear as a witness. To that extent, we could just ignore it, but that's not what we are doing. The Chamber will seek that you will be assisted in getting counsel being present in court with the limited role of advising you on your position as a witness, and to have that done as quickly as possible, but that we would start your testimony today. Now, with efforts taken by everyone, it might be that tomorrow already there could be someone sitting next to you. The Chamber has instructed that OLAD and the victims and witness section will be consulted on the matter, but the Chamber sees no reason to delay the start of your testimony. The Chamber has invited the party that was calling you not to put -- not to start your testimony with any matter that might even come close to any such situation as I just described. That is, that there would be an objective concern about incriminating yourself by answering a question. Therefore, under those circumstances, the Chamber will invite you to make a solemn declaration. We'll start with your testimony, and, at the same time, if you express your continued wish to be assisted by counsel, or counsel being present, the Chamber will certainly promote that that is in effect as soon as possible. And that is the present situation. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is quite clear to me. Based on my conversations with my lawyers, nobody invited them here. One of them is in possession of a visa; the other one isn't. I don't see where this misunderstanding arose. They were corresponding with the Defence, and I don't see why I should be made an exception of. Others testified based on a subpoena or not based on a subpoena, but with the presence of their counsel. I do wish to testify. Of course, under the proviso that you would be drawing my attention so as not to say anything that might harm me, but I think the rules should be applied. I think quite a few exceptions were already made at my expense before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no rule that entitles you to be assisted by counsel. Counsel have had an opportunity since they were aware that you would be called to testify for weeks. We have not heard of any application. They have not contacted the Chamber. Therefore, there's no rule that you are entitled to be assisted by counsel as a witness. So, therefore, the Chamber is not making any exception to the rule. You and possible counsel have not addressed the Chamber with any request up till this moment which is common in those circumstances, where, as a matter of fact, an exception is made to the general rule. The general rule is that the witness comes to this court, answers questions, and is in no way assisted by counsel. That is the general rule. And if you wanted an exception to be made, you should have taken action, or your lawyers should have taken action. At the same time I add to this, that in order to accommodate your concerns, I instructed the staff to be in touch with VWS and OLAD to see whether they can arrange for either your counsel or your counsel instructing a counsel who is on duty and who could be present. So if you say that you would prefer that counsel is present in court for you, just tell us at this moment, and the Chamber will do everything that this wish can be met. If that is your wish, and I do understand it is, then the Chamber staff will work on it from this very moment. At the same time, I add to this, that the Chamber has asked Mr. Misetic, who will examine you, to not deal with any matter that might even come close to matters that could incriminate yourself. So I take it that the questions today will be not touching upon these matters. And it could well be that tomorrow your wish could already be met, but we start today. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm counting on the proceedings being fair here and that everything will be in order. I would have preferred my counsel to be here. I am aware of the fact that individuals were brought over here from Austria and other countries and appeared here in the presence of their counsel. Even if I am convicted, I haven't lost my right to having my counsel here. I might give an answer that is not in my best interest under the influence of my emotions. I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you one thing very clear. Even if counsel is present, you will not be able to consult with counsel, apart from here in the courtroom, because counsel is not allowed to discuss with you or to speak with you about the substance of your testimony. There is only one thing whether it is in your best interests or not, the only thing we expect you to do is to give answers in accordance with the truth, nothing else. Whether it is favourable, whether it is unfavourable. Only if you would have to fear that the answer would tend to incriminate yourself, under those circumstances we'll consider whether the obligation to answer the question still exists or not. And that's the matter on which you could consult with counsel, if present in court, not on the substance of the questions and answers. I'm happy to hear that you expect these proceedings to be fair, not only in respect of the accused but that we would also be fair to witnesses. That's exactly the reason why I explained to you in detail not only what your duties are but also what your rights are in this respect. Then I would like to invite to you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. Could you please stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrksic. Please be seated. I'm addressing you as Mr. Mrksic, but I take it that the first question of Mr. Misetic will be to state your full name for the record. Yes, Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Mr. Misetic starts with his questions if I can have a minute or two. I said that new methods were being applied in relation to me. What I meant to say was that I had a similar problem as that of Mr. Misetic in my own case, (redacted) was supposed to appear as a witness, a subpoena was issued which was not followed up on. That's why I chose the course of action I did. I waited for the subpoena. The Tribunal seemed to have exerted some pressure, and then I was being told that I should appear or shouldn't appear, and I didn't think that my questions would be threatened. Likewise, a doctor under instructions that he received burst into my room and told me that I had to urgently undergo a medical checkup for the purposes of the subpoena. I agreed to that. However, they did not follow up on this. Nobody conducted me later on. I was confronted by an official who showed up with a subpoena to sign for me, and I asked about my lawyers. I wasn't told anything other than I was to appear here the following day. I was hoping that my counsel would be here, but since they are not, I can tell you that I will answer your questions, and I will speak the truth and nothing but the truth. Now that the situation has arose, let me tell you that it's been 14 years that I've carried this burden within me. I have never testified in the meantime; I haven't given any statements to the press or television. I am a man who was silent for a very long time, and I would not wish to bring harm to anyone now. Hence, my position is a difficult one, and you should be the one to pay attention to what it is that I'm doing because you have agreed to the situation where my counsel is not present here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There's a name that was mentioned that should be redacted that was a protected witness in the other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't aware of that. Mr. Registrar, 49, line 9, I take it. At not your name, Mr. Misetic, which also appears on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I need protection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot that he was a protected witness. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please carefully listen to the questions put to you by Mr. Misetic and answer them and try to focus specifically on what is asked. I take it that you are aware that Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. He called you as a witness, and he will be the first to examine you. And let me assure you the Chamber is aware that it might not be easy for you. That doesn't change that much the situation, but be confident that we are aware of that. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: My name is Mile Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me start off by saying --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-general in retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me start off by saying that it is my intention that this is as least stressful as possible for you. If at any moment you don't feel well, you should immediately tell the Presiding Judge. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to start by asking you some preliminary questions. First, could you tell us and tell the Court how you -- when you became the Chief of Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I think that this was after the fall of Western Slavonia, when the commander Celeketic was replaced. They were looking for an individual who would create a new climate of safety and security among the people who were instilled with great fear, an individual who would be able to exert influence on the top leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to change their conduct and to focus on the process of finding the final settlement to the crisis in Croatia. It was a very difficult process. I was called over special telephone lines home and persuaded into accepting this duty knowing in advance that it was going to be a very difficult and responsible position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just state that if you could focus your answers to the specific questions, we're going to have plenty time to get into the details as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But it will be easier if you focus on the specific question. So if you could next tell us, where were you physically located when you were first asked to become the Chief of Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the army of Serbian Krajina. Previously I was assistant chief for land forces of the army of the SRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Montenegro. Shortly before these developments, I was advisor to the defence minister. That's to say between February 1995 and May, when I took up my duty as the commander of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Earlier on if you're interested in the history, I was the commander of the special corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Misetic just asked you where were you when you were first asked --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might interrupt you a couple of times. Again, sometimes questions are far more simple than you think they are. Just where were you, when was it. And if Mr. Misetic wants to know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know how it is. We want to say as much as we can, so I apologise that I'm not keeping within the time-frame that you have in mind, and I hope that you will get back to some issues, some questions. I have no experience whatsoever with testifying. I have never even appeared in court for a traffic incident, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Understood. And I think you will get used to it as we go along. Please, can you clarify, you were the advisor to the minister of defence of which country before you took up your post as commander of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I that I was Serbia and Montenegro at the time. The names changed rather frequently. Whether it was still the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Serbia and Montenegro, I'm really not sure anymore. Let's leave this to history. I think Montenegro was still part at the time of that Yugoslavia. Or perhaps it was the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who approached you about leaving your post as the assistant -- sorry, advisor to the minister of defence of the FRY to become the commander of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I was approached by the chief of the General Staff, or, rather, by the minister who actually relayed the request of the Chief of Staff. I was invited to a meeting, and then minister told me, actually, he told me I should go to a meeting. I think the meeting was at Dedinje, a meeting with President Milosevic where I also -- where also was the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Martic, who was in a difficult emotional situation -- condition, because of the fall of Western Slavonia and everything that was going on. And the request was that I should be appointed the commander and Celeketic replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said you were approached by the chief of the General Staff. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was he who actually told me anything -- or rather the minister, the minister of defence was the one who actually told me to go to this meeting. I can't say for sure now, but the chief of the General Staff at the time was General Perisic, Colonel Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: And the minister of defence was the late Pavle Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did they explain to you what they wanted you to do at this meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, there was only an attempt to actually get me to accept this. They were saying how they needed the best people in order to resolve this issue, because panic had set in among the people after Western Slavonia. So they were looking for a personality, a person who would be acceptable both to the fighters and to the population there, and also acceptable to the leadership, of course, and, of course, President Milosevic, the late President Milosevic, was also there. He said, We've selected the best men we could find.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now what were you told at this meeting was your task, if you accepted this position.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Well, at this meeting, I did not accept this new post, and there was no mention of what the tasks would be. The only discussion was about how to -- how can I explain this to you? How to actually get me to accept this role. So this was not the final meeting. There were three or four following this, and there as lot of phone calls. They also called me at home. There were also private phone calls, so that in the end I realised that I would have to go there. As for the tasks, I was issued assignments at another meeting, what it was I was supposed to do and how. And that is precisely what I would like to talk about here, because this has been a heavy burden on my mind and no one has ever asked about this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will get to that question in a few minutes. Let me ask you, though, preliminarily, can you explain to us why or what -- what was your understanding of why Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Perisic would be involved in deciding who would be the commander of the ARSK? Why was that decision being taken in the ...

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if I may address you in that way, let me say this. They were not the ones who were to decide on this. Because under the law they did not have the authority to send me to the territory of another republic or state unless I accepted this. So Martic was the final instance who was supposed to decide on this. He was the one who actually submitted the request. And because I was born in that area, I -- I hail from that area, and I knew the functions that I had been on earlier, they knew that I was the only man who could have an influence on the people who lived there. So Martic was the one who asked for this. As for them, they really weren't happy about having to let go of their own personnel. And also, it was in their interest to stabilize the situation and avoid going into war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mrksic, General Mrksic, let me show awe document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, this is 65 ter 1D1077, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm going to show you is a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Perisic on the 18th of May, and I will alert the Chamber already that I, just as I was standing here, noted a translation issue, the English translation. But, Mr. General Mrksic, you will understand it in the original. If we go down a little bit on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the transcript been provided to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 18th of May, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about intercepted telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not playing the audio, I'm just -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not playing the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, 18th of May. And if you see M, I believe, refers to --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. M refers to Mr. - let me see - Mr. Perisic, and S is Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go down and read this, they greet each other. And then it says -- S says: "Look I have just received a report. Martic has gone completely mad." And then it says: "Yes" --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask your permission if I could read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would read it out the relevant portion slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next sentence says: [Interpretation] "He has gone mad after he heard of the appointment of Mrksic." [In English] Now, and then it goes on. Let me finish reading the relevant portions to you, and then I will ask for your comments. He says: "Now he does not know how to evade his involvement. He has agreed with Karadzic to pursue some sort of urgent unification so that Karadzic would become president and Martic an army commander. Thus, they would eliminate both Mrksic and Mladic with Krajisnik as prime minister." And then if we turn the page in English, please --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and in the B/C/S. It says: M, again, is Mr. Perisic: "Here's what we will do. I want Mrksic" --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean M is Perisic? Oh, Momcilo you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. "Here's what we will do. I want Mrksic in my office tomorrow at 7.00. "Very well. Because is he going to this assembly meeting there. You know where?"

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: That's right. This would have been either Borovo Selo or Dalj. That's where I was appointed to be commander of the assembly. Martic was only the proposer. He proposed to the assembly; he did not appoint anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to wait until Mr. Misetic -- he is just reading at this moment to make you acquainted with the text, and then he will ask a question which could be anything. But wait until he has put his question to you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now S continues on a little bit lower and says: "And tell Mile not to worry. The assembly will be all right. He will ... the government will be all right, and none of his ramblings [sic] will have any consequences."

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: What does he mean -- I mean whom does he mean when he says ramblings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would wait until the question would be put to you. You can ask if you do not understand, but wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page one more time. Right in the middle of the page it says: "Right. This is what I will do with Loncar, and you need not worry. I will" -- And then S for Slobodan, says: "Tell him to communicate with no one else but Mrksic and not to accept any orders from Martic." Now my question to you is: At this time do you recall having conversations with either Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Perisic or both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't necessarily have a problem with this particular question, but I do want to object to the procedure of putting a document to a witness on direct examination, reading it to him. There's been no foundation for the document itself. Representations have been made about who is speaking in it, what they are saying. I think that this is it leading the witness in an inappropriate way. He should be asked, first of all, if he is aware of this conversation, and he should be asked before being shown the document questions regarding what's in it before being introduced to what other people have said about a matter with which he is going to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you is said you have no objection to this question. I think what you said is well understood by Mr. Misetic. I cannot exactly know whether it was covered already by the earlier question, yes or no. But since there is no objection against this question, the witness may answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask that preliminary question, and then I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you had any conversations at that point in time with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, or Mr. Misetic, I have no idea what you're showing me here. This is the first time that I see this. Nor did I ever have occasion to hear of these conversations at an assembly session, I was approached by a man who told me to show up at the command post.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear at what place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then I got there they told me go to Karadjordjevo; the president is waiting for you there. President Milosevic. And I'm glad you put this question because that is exactly what I would want to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason I put this to him is because the witness has testified that he was chosen by Mr. Martic. I have already prepared on the issue of leading. I, just for the record, given the circumstances here, call on the -- or just cite to the decision of the Appeals Chamber of 1 February 2008 decision on appeals against decision on impeachment of a party's own witness and ask that if this objection is going to continue that the Appeals Chamber's ruling there about the latitude given in direct examination on a case-by-case, question-by-question basis apply here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a law which says that the Court knows the laws, but it is good that you have drawn our attention to a specific decision. Mr. Russo, I take it that you have some understanding for the position of the Defence at this moment who has had no opportunity to speak with the witness before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Let me say first, I'm not familiar with this particular decision. I'm aware that the Chamber certainly has the authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, I'm more or less -- I was -- always, I'm serious, but I think I expressed that I had no vivid knowledge of this decision right at the spot. So, therefore, we will look at it. And if you do the same, then we will see how we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. Up to the point where the matter is decided, I do have a standing objection to this process of putting documents to a witness on direct examination which are leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record, and as I said before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. And I need to respond to one other matter. In terms of the procedure and fairness, I would -- if we're going to develop with this issue, what the Prosecution did in its case in chief was put documents to witnesses, put it in a 92 ter, and then get around the leading issue by saying it is in his 92 ter. So given that we have had no opportunity to take a 92 ter, we think that, in terms of fairness, that should be also taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll further consider the matter, and the standing objection is on the record, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I will object for lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1508, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you referred to a meeting of the Assembly. Can you tell us what transpired at that meeting, in terms of your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was some discussion on the responsibility of Mikelic for the fall of Western Slavonia and Celeketic's responsibility. But all I recall about myself was that I was appointed commander, and I also remember that I was told after this session of parliament that I should go to the Karadjordjevo villa where President Milosevic was, that he was awaiting me. And I went there with my security right away for a conversation, and the two of us spent some two hours in conversation, maybe even longer, and that is what I would like to talk about here. Because that was the key conversation, that conversation between us was key for me and for everything that happened afterwards, and yet there have been no documents shown or any notes shown from the meeting. It says here that Martic was not in favour of my appointment. I think that's what you were trying to show. There were some documents where he was actually complaining about my appointment. That is true. However, he was forced by circumstance to accept me because he knew, as the previous commanders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He knew as -- if you could just finish that sentence. He knew as the previous commanders were, what?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Well, he knew that I was a different type of commander, because with previous commanders there were issues. He knew that I was a professional who would not really meddle in political affairs; I would just asked for assignments to be carried out; and I would impose issues that had to be resolved. And I did not have any kind of problem with figures of authority, Milosevic, or Karadzic, or Mladic, or anyone. For me, the only authority was the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for our communication, if I put up my hand, I'm trying to signal to you if could you stop, so that the translators can finish, and I will put another question to you, okay? Now let's talk about this meeting that you have brought up with President Milosevic in Karadjordjevo. First can you tell us when that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That conversation took place right after the Assembly session. Well, it could have been what, some two hours that it took me to get to Karadjordjevo from Borovo Selo. I went -- we travelled via Ilok. I think the session was at that afternoon, maybe around noon. I can't tell you exactly. I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, I want to ask you two things. First, not to give any details you were not asked for, because the question was when that conversation took place. Now you are telling us by what route you went there, which Mr. Misetic might not be interested in. So just say two hours after the Assembly meeting, or on the 24th of May at 3.00 in the afternoon. But just focus your answer on the question; that's one. Second is that you're speaking very quickly. Could I ask you to slow down; that's one. And also to make a short break between question and answer. If you have finished your answer, it takes a while before it is translated for us. So Mr. Misetic then waits until the translation is finished and then puts his next question to you. Now, if you start adding anything to your answer while Mr. Misetic is still waiting for the translation to be finished, then the interpreters cannot follow us anymore. And apart from that, Mr. Misetic may be satisfied with your answer already and would like to put his next question to you. Could you please try to keep that in mind? Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting with President Milosevic in Karadjordjevo, what did President Milosevic tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: President Milosevic, as far as I can recall, because I don't have any documents or any papers, I had to return all those after the fall of the Krajina. I don't have any official notes and the rest. But the essence was the following. As I had already been sent there earlier before that Assembly session and I was advised of the situation in Krajina because I received reports from different corps, I already knew what the situation was like there, and I could talk about it with him. So the -- the gist was this. That this issue could no longer be resolved by military means. That it would have to be resolved by political means. Western Slavonia showed that the Croatian forces had grown to such an extent that the balance of power had changed, that we -- that we had to actually try to influence the -- the perceptions among our leaders and also the understanding that the people had on the situation on the ground and to try to find a situation -- to try to make the people realize that they would have to accommodate the other side and stay there. And then I asked him, Well, how do we do this? And he said, The leaders there, the president and also Mikelic, the president of parliament, who was supposed to retire at the time, but that I should talk to them and by -- in exerting my authority to try to prevent the unification of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska, because this is something that is unacceptable under some international standards, and it would only be actually throwing sand in the eyes of the people. And that I should take immediate action within the army so that the people would change their intentions, because they had already packed for leaving. So what he was telling me basically was, Please try and do whatever you can so that the people would again trust the army. So he said, Here, you have five to six months. You will have up to November to create this new atmosphere within the army. And I had intended to create various corps and that each corps should have a reserve brigade. And it was important to understand that it was not logistically possible to go into war, it was not reasonable, that we would have to try to find other methods so that people can live together there. Milosevic told me, Mile, I know that Western Slavonia is far, and I know that Knin and Vukovar are very far. I will -- I want you to take care of these 4th Corps. And I will give the same assignment so these other commanders. So my job was, You are supposed to change the perception among the people of the role of the army. And once that happens, then it is easy to persuade the people to stay. And then he told me -- and then he told me, Just put your paw on all TV programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's get to this then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D923, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, I'm going to show you a document on the screen. Do you recall filing a report after Operation Storm to the chief of the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army about the activities of the RSK from 4 August to 10 August 1995? If we could turn to the last page so you can see the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes. But could you just scroll it to the left so that can I see who actually drafted this document. This is my signature, but they wouldn't dare submit a document of this type for me to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, where were you on the 26th of August --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: And I will tell you immediately why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: The 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I was in Banja Luka. But why am I saying this? Well, I'm saying this because of other documents that you might show here, and there will be various documents bearing my signature. But let me say this: I am a professional, a general who had been schooled and appointed to the highest duties. It is absolutely unthinkable that a document should be signed by me without indication as to who had drafted it and who had typed it. Anyone who had gone through some schooling would know this, so this would not happen, not even to a squad leader in my army. Now as for the contents, we can discuss it if I recall what it is that it's talking about. But, first of all, we have to establish whether is this actually my document, because in technical terms, in the terms of its form, it is not a document -- it is impossible this is a document that I would have signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir. Did you file a report after Operation Storm to the chief of the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: We submitted not only reports but entire analyses produced by a whole team. It's not a -- an insignificant matter to lose a war, to lose a territory, and to lose a people. We did this job seriously. And it was a study, even.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at this document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if you look at section 1, it says: "Situation within the SVK, conditions and characteristics of the situation preceding the aggression?" Now, it says in the first paragraph: "In June there was a day and night work on reorganizing the existing military organisation and establishing new units out of military conscripts who were being brought from the territory of the FRY." Now, is that statement there accurate? Were you in fact working day and night to re-organise the military and establish new units from military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We were reorganizing the situation as it was. I apologise, may I explain this. When I got there, I analysed -- This will save you additional questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will ask you the questions, and I'm sure you will have an opportunity to provide the information you wish. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic -- Mr. Misetic, I'm at the same time looking at the clock. Could you find within the next three or four minutes a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, if we turn the page in the English, and I think it's still the same in the B/C/S. It says: "Strengthening of the established organisation and making it capable of carrying out combat activities required a minimum time-period of two to three months (the reorganisation of the SVK, which had already started was planned to conclude until the beginning of October, at the latest)." Can you tell us briefly in just a few minutes - and we will pick up on it after the break - what you were doing specifically in terms of reorganisation that was going to be completed at the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Specifically, we were working toward creating a professional army, the sort of army that Croatia and Serbia have today. The sort of army that would not be linked to their land -- whatever. An army that would be capable of deploying to Grahovo, to other areas that were part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. This was the -- this referred to the forces that were under my command. The highest quality personnel fled as early as in 1994, 1995 to Serbia and to engage in smuggling. Let me just tell what you the reorganisation consisted of. Certain tactical groups were supposed to be formed up to the level of brigades within the corps that were supposed to solve specific problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, it is now that we have received the interpretation of your words. We would rather not miss a word of what you say, so if you slow down your speed of speech that would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do recall at my trial that we kept on slowing witnesses down, and I always wondered how it was that they would never understand that they should slow down, so I do apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a good time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a good time for a break. We will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you restart, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Mrksic, if everything goes well, tomorrow - and let me just see, we are sitting, Mr. Registrar, afternoon? Morning - that somewhere during tomorrow morning, that counsel will arrive that could then further be present with this limited role, but that's -- there's a fair chance that that will happen. He might not be there in the beginning of the morning but perhaps at the end of the morning session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Domazet. Who is it you are referring to? Your Honour, who do you have in mind, Domazet or Vasic, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Domazet, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, picking up where we left off about this reorganisation. Do you know what the special purposes corps was in the ARSK, and can you tell us how that was created?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the special purpose corps was named a corps, but far be it that it was a corps. You know that corps normally have their AORs. It had few men, but it was very efficient. Had the top notch weaponry, 94 guns at its disposal, the extent of which the RSK had at the time. You see when I came to the Krajina to tour the army, I saw the M84 tanks, and they were the cutting edge technology. And I suggested to the Supreme Defence Council that I should build up the forces in an area, and I meant tanks, APCs, 130-millimetre artillery, multi-barrel rocket launchers, Orkans, Dvinas, Nevas, all these systems, which left outside the control, could be very dangerous. And a brigade was formed from the ranks of the very best infantry men in order to provide technical support to the hardware. I tried to make sure that professional employment contracts were set up, and by the St. Vitus Day, the corps was in fact formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what were you going to use that corps for?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: The corps's purpose was a preventative one. Should there be a sudden incursion or advancement as happened in Western Slavonia, it should be there to stop the advancement. Its significance was more a psychological one, to restore the confidence of the people into the army, to reassure them that they could remain there, and to show both to the international community and the Republic of Croatia that we were prepared to engage in negotiations and not in a war. The purpose was to make sure that negotiations were embarked on, and not military activity. That's why I set it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the Pauk command was?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think that this fell within the zone. It opens up different issues that have nothing to do with this. I can tell you that the first combat experience that the corps had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply was whether you know what the Pauk command was. If you know, say yes; if you don't know, say no. Whether it's a different issue or not, that's for Mr. Misetic to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Misetic, I did hear of the Pauk command which was part of western Bosnia, within the area of Fikret Abdic. It had not been subordinated to me until the start of combat activities in western Bosnia which was sometime in the month of July, the objective of that activity being that certain villages that were part of the Cazin Krajina or, rather, they were on the fringes of the Cazin Krajina and wanted to come under his command, Abdic's command, it was to -- to that end that these forces were used. The Pauk command and Fikret's forces seized the territories I referred to, and made sure that the people who occupied the area joined their side. That particular command was there before I came into the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now approximately that we've received the interpretation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What units comprised the Pauk command or were under the command of Pauk?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Either the command or the forces involved is something that I never had occasion to learn. These were units under the command of Fikret Abdic. They were subject to a special regime, and I cannot tell you anything about it. I know that some 10.000 men were involved. That's what I was told, that that was manpower I could count on. But that's quite a different topic that we can broach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, were you aware of any units of the Serbian SDB under Frenki Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic operating in the territory of the Pauk command?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there were units there. There were only individuals who were commanders of these units who were under Fikret Abdic. And I'm sure those who were in the legion among you know that, that these were merely units deployed in an area and cooperating. They disagreed with the policies of the 5th Corps. I don't know who personally who these persons were. I may have heard about them, but I didn't inquire about that; I wasn't interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mrksic, do you recall being in Belgrade at the end of June and attending any meetings at which Mr. Perisic, Mr. Milosevic, Ratko Mladic, and Jovica Stanisic were present, along with you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: There were meetings. I don't know what you have in mind. There was one meeting where a decision was taken to launch an action to -- involving Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what exactly.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: We did plan an operation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: However, this had -- [Previous translation continues] ... nothing to do with the Dalmatian -- I could testify about that on some other occasion, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You seem to be under the impression, and it hasn't been picked up by the translation, that you get to decide what is relevant to General Gotovina's case. And if you would please simply answer the questions that I put to you, and if is there is something outside of the indictment, our colleagues on the Prosecution will be sure to rise on their feet and object. But in the meantime, if you would please answer my questions, I would appreciate it. Now at this meeting or meetings that you reference at the end of June, do you recall Mr. Stanisic indicating that he had any forces under his command, that he could send to assist in this operation that you have now referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I would have to have a look. I'm not familiar with the minutes. I don't have the documents, and there were several such meetings. I only know that the general position was that this action should be launched in order for more room for manoeuvre to be created for Fikret Abdic so that the people could join him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I will show you some notes from that meeting in a minute. But what I'd like to know right now is what you recollect. And in those meetings concerning the Pauk command an operations in western Bosnia, do you recall you committing forces of the ARSK in that operation in the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I controlled my forces, and over Krslja, I exerted pressure in order for them to carry out their objectives. That's why the special purpose corps was there. The forces came from the direction of Kladusa and from the mountain, and they were Muslim forces that were under the Pauk command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition to forces that you were commanding, were there also forces sent from the Serbian SDB?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There was some talk of it, of some forces that may have come from Eastern Slavonia or from Republika Srpska, from MUP, but they did not come in my AOR; they came in the AOR of Kladusa. And I wasn't able to know what was going on there. I was at the command post of Slunj, and Krslja is right across the Korana. So I can't tell you what it was that happened in their area. It was a separate system that we did not meddle with that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I do. He is here in the detention as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you know Frenki Simatovic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I did. But I did not see him in 1995. I would see him more often in 1994 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with Frenki Simatovic in 1995 by telephone or other means?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did Frenki Simatovic --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I had such powers as did not require me to call Frenki or have any dealings with him. There was General Novakovic who was in Pauk coordinating matters. Cedo Bulat as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, what was Frenki Simatovic, in 1995, in your understanding, what was his function?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I think he was one of the assistants in the DB sector for these -- well, I don't know what sort of sectors they had there. He was in one of the sectors. He was the assistant there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, the DB sector of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Serbia, Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this sector, did it involve having combat units?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were some combat units that were called red berets or something of that sort. These were special units carrying out specific assignments. Fikret Abdic could not have set up an army on his own without these specialists who were charged with specific assignments. What their strength was, I didn't know, and I didn't ask about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Milorad Ulemek Legija is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, Legia, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you know -- I'm sorry, did you communicate Milorad Ulemek Legija in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: He was there when the assignment for action called Sword much [as interpreted] was issued. This was in the month of July. He was there to receive assignments. I asked him how would he be carrying out assignments, and he said that there, in the Foreign Legion, he only knew of a squad. He didn't know how he should be issuing these assignments to brigades. And he was part of Fikret Abdic's forces at the time. And his attitude toward the assignment was very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, who, under whose command was Milorad Ulemek Legija?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: He was under Pauk's command. It was General Novakovic and Bulat. As for them, they were subject to professional monitoring from, probably in addition to Fikret Abdic's staff, somebody from the DB. I don't know who and when they came. But this was a separate structure. It was in Kladusa, whereas I was in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At this meeting or meetings in Belgrade at the end of June 1995, do you recall why this operation was being launched? Any discussion of why it was being launched?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The operation was launched, and I was supposed to accompany the forces that I formed. You didn't allow me to tell you what it was that I did concerning the army, and I hope you will, because it will prove important for some other matters that will come up later. And I am expecting these questions. We were supposed to start developing a plan to sever the forces in Livanjsko Polje, and a counterattack was supposed to be carried there by the forces of Republika Srpska and the RSK jointly in order to prevent Knin from being cut off which in fact happened. However, the VRS had some other priorities, I don't know which, and they gave up on this participation. Whereas, I wasn't able to deploy in their area because there was General Milovanovic there and a major, a lady, who told me that I was not entitled to go into the their AOR. They only said, Just give me a unit, give me some hardware, and whatever they -- whatever we managed to seize during the day, they would then lose during the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we would have two steps forward; one step back. And I was angry at the time because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, for the purposes of the proceedings, if I could avoid directing to your comments sitting to people behind me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We are soldiers. We understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as discipline is concerned, I take it that reducing the speed of speech will be part of your discipline now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes. Thank you. [Interpretation] Just caution me, and I will obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The translation was, If you issue a disciplinary measure, I will obey it. But that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General, were you sensing that you understand my questions in English. And for the purpose of the interpreters in the booth and the transcribers, you still need to wait for the translation to finish in your ears so that you start with your answer. Now, let's go back to what my original question was, which is: Why were you launching an operation against the Bihac pocket, or in the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't launch the operation. The Bihac pocket was secondary to my priorities, one of which was Dinara, as well as Livno and Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to this report, and I'll maybe help you get to where the specific question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this operation, if you were to follow the context of what precedes the paragraph starts: "The initiation of the operations ..." It says: "The initiation of the operations against the 5th Muslim Corps" -- and that would be the corps in the Bihac pocket; correct? Do you have this in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The top of page two in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The 5th Muslim Corps is the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina Corps in the Bihac Pocket; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now it says: "The initiation of the operations against the 5th Muslim Corps, without the necessary readiness, particularly damaged the SVK, which was always, as if according to some rule, being pushed into the fighting for the territories of western Bosnia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who's pushing the ARSK to fight for the territories of western Bosnia? What I don't understand about this paragraph is you are the commander of the Main Staff of the ARSK. So who's pushing to fight for the territories of western Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: A meeting was held in Belgrade attended by Fikret Abdic, and, as you say, President Milosevic, and I believe there was also Perisic, and someone else was there from Republika Srpska as well - I was there as well - where I raised as the major issue, the axis across the Dinara. However, a conclusion was arrived, and somebody told Fikret Abdic that the inhabitants of the areas on the fringes of Cazin could hardly wait for an action to be launched in order for them to join his side by plebescite. It was concluded at the time that this would help the creation of -- you know, that the Republic of Serbian Krajina was thinnest in the stretch from Ogulin toward Bihac. It wasn't an inhabited area, and it was not difficult to capture. It would only take a day. And if we look at the defence of the RSK on the operative level and in terms of any surprise, hinterland had to be assured so that he would have your back covered. Because it was difficult for us to hold the line that was in front of us, and let alone the line that faced the 5th Corp. For this reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have pressed yourself on for 15 lines. I still do not know who was pushing. You're referred to meeting; was someone at the meeting pushing, and, if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the request of Fikret Abdic, it was President Milosevic who took up the position that the matter should be resolved and that they should be helped. And he said, Mile, go over there. Once this issue has been settled, go over there and see what you request do about the Dinara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer seems to be, Who was pushing? It was Fikret Abdic who got the support of Mr. Milosevic; they pushed it. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Fikret Abdic could not issue commands to me. He could submit a request to President Milosevic who would then call Martic and so on, including me, and then a decision could be made of that -- to that effect. That decision was also in our favour because I needed to get some security for my rear so I needed some depth of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still trying to understand. Was it those at the meeting who were pushing, as it was reported? Is that how I have to understand your answer? Because that's the simple question. In the report it says that -- and let me take it back for a second. It was read to you by Mr. Misetic that you were -- the ARSK was pushed to fight for the territories of western Bosnia. Is now your answer that those who pushed you were those present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Try to focus, because you explained to us whether -- what it was good for to do it, many other things. But Mr. Misetic just wants to know who pushed you. And the answer could be given in two or three lines: At a meeting in Belgrade where those and those and those were present. We were pushed, or the ARSK was pushed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't remember who all were present there. Maybe you can read the names out to me and then maybe that will help jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, let me see if we can refresh your memory, General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this is Exhibit D1465.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I noted that 1D1077, you did not tender that. Was that your intention? That's the transcript, Perisic/Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe you MFI'd that one, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that one was MFI'd. Yes, I see that. Yes, it has been MFI'd. Yes as D1508. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Mrksic, this is the diary of Ratko Mladic which -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to B/C/S page 206 and English page 201, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is -- you can see on the left-hand part of your screen, a meeting purported to be on the 29th of June, 1995 -- I'll wait for the English translation to be uploaded. There we go. BGD, Belgrade, it was in the evening at 2110, and it says that present at the meeting are Milosevic, Bulatovic, Perisic, Mrksic, and presumably Mladic is the person taking the notes. If you look through these notes, it is says SM, which by the initials, would seem to be Slobodan Milosevic. "Now have you stopped the Croat Muslim offensive. We helped you, but we are at our last gasp. "Republika Srpska is ensured, we must seal it and place emphasis on the RSK and defend it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 201 in the English. I believe if we can turn the page in the B/C/S; perhaps 2 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm a bit lost. I'm now at 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to we were in the English and go two pages forward. I apologise. I'm using a different pagination in my notes. I believe it would be page 203. Perhaps page 208 in the B/C/S. That's it. Now, there's an entry -- I have to trust that the B/C/S is reflecting this accurately. I don't read Cyrillic, Mr. President, so ... okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "We must install RS and then defend the RSK. "What would you give them, I ask him." SM: "I would give Vogosca and Ilijas." Now, General Mrksic, without much detail, can you tell the Court where are Vogosca and Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Vogosca and Ilijas were Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on: "They need a link with Sarajevo, Zenica, and Tuzla. We would enlarge on account of Fikret. I would not touch the enclaves; they are islands which will run out." Now, do you recall being present at a meeting where this conversation -- is this the meeting that you were talking about, a conversation to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there were a number of meetings, and I can't recall whether this was at this particular meeting. There was a meeting, I remember, but what is written down here, that's not what transpired at the meeting. There was a meeting which I attended, where there was an inform conversation, and I wasn't even invited to the meeting. I was invited once it was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you recall -- let me just ask the question. Do you recall being present at a meeting in Belgrade where Mr. Milosevic was present, Mr. Perisic was present, Mr. Mladic was present, and you were present at which there was a discussion about giving Vogosca and Ilijas an enlarging on account of Fikret?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I did not attend a meeting where that was discussed. The meeting where I was, was an informal meeting. It was a relaxed atmosphere. It was in the evening. And there was no mention of seeding territory and so on and so forth. President Milosevic and Mladic bantered. There were discussing -- they were saying something about the microphone, the tape-recorder, and so on and so forth. So it didn't really look like a meeting, nor were any notes kept. I didn't see anyone keeping any notes, nor did I write anything down in my notebook, nor did I get any assignments. It was just an informal meeting, and I noticed that what was said in this informal atmosphere was that mile should be given some help in order to survive there. But I heard nothing of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is three pages forward in the English, Mr. Registrar. This is it another meeting, the 30th of June, 1995. It's page 211 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which I find, at least, the witness being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the notes. Page 206 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 206 out of 334, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrksic, this is 30 June 1995. It says it's a meeting with President Milosevic at the Yugoslav Army General Staff. And then President Milosevic: "I called FA," Fikret Abdic, "to tell us what is new in the Bihac pocket. That is very important for us. We must do something so he can take Cazin. And then it will be easier later. And then FA proceeds to apparently speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's an entry that says: "Legija and Bozovic had contact with Nanic through a Motorola. We could take Cazin in two weeks if we had 1500 men." Now, first can you tell the Court who Bozovic is?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Bozovic was at the same level as this other guy, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: As Legija, yes. The two of them were representatives of two structures; they were instructors, as it were. I think this is according to the legion code. So they were instructors in the army of Fikret Abdic and each of them had under their control one and a half to two brigades and conducted operations with him, yes, he was an instructor. And whenever it was necessary to get an assignment for Pauk, they would be the ones who would attend. And they would just convey that information to Fikret Abdic. He was not present. And this Nanic guy, he was some sort of official from the 5th Corps, but I don't know exactly what he was, but I heard that later on he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was Jovica Stanisic present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know if his name is mentioned here in the notes. I can't really recall on my own, but if it is in the notes, then we should believe it; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you go to the next sentence it says JS. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, probably Jovica Stanisic. JS. Well, those are his initials. I assume that probably that is him. And if we can see from the notes that he took part in this discussion, I can't really -- I can't really remember the -- there were five to six men. I can't remember exact who was there and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, I ask because that sentence says: "JS: Which forces can Mr. Mrksic engage?" And then what about the police from Banja Luka, et cetera. And then it goes on. And you have mentioned some of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You've talked about a discussion, I believe earlier in your testimony in this session, about you were asked to go in the Bihac pocket, but you were talking about Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to that page --

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, my plan was to -- Livno, Livno was my plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you look at -- in the middle of this page, SM, which again is presumably Slobodan Milosevic. "I think it is important to resolve the 5th Corps as soon as possible and then to try cutting off near Livno." Do you recall, as part of the conversation, that Mr. Milosevic said this?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: I think that he did say that, because I kept insisting on the importance of Livno. I considered that Livno was of crucial importance for the -- for Republika Srpska. So the Dinara and not the 5th Corp. And he probably said that in order to actually satisfy both needs, but Republika Srpska failed completely in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Explain to the Chamber why Livno was of crucial importance.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Well, when I say Livno, I don't mean that we would attack the town of Livno. Rather, we would come in contact with the forces at Livanjsko Polje so that the axis, Knin-Drvar could no longer be threatened. We I think in this way we would shift the front line, and this would return -- in this way the situation it the Dinara would be reverted to where it was in 1994, mid-1994. So when I say that communications have improved up there, there's work being done, we can hear machines doing work, an attack is being prepared from the rear, the -- the people from Republika Srpska did not heed my words. They didn't consider them seriously enough, especially --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes that the name was Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Especially Milovanovic did not believe this, but of course he proceeded to something else and now -- and then he would become a senator in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this, sir. You talk about -- you wanted to return the situation to where it was in mid-1994. Was it part of your plan -- we saw earlier that you had a plan to improve the ARSK by early October. Was it part of your overall plan to militarily return the situation to back -- back to the way it was in the middle of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: It was our idea to -- in political terms and in terms of organisation, we would unify the will of the people and the politicians and secure Republika Srpska without relying on Serbia because it was clear to us that we won't get any help from the Republic of Serbia. And I would like to tell this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... political question now. I'm asking you strictly militarily, from a military perspective.

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, militarily, that's what my answer refers to, if you just are willing to hear me out. In other words, to use our own forces, and relying on our own forces only, to force our politicians to proceed to a peaceful resolution of the issue in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is speaking too fast and cannot be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you slowly repeat the last part of your answer, Mr. Mrksic, because we're missing your words if you speak too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will try and slow down. And I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your answer was, I wanted to return the front lines to where they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I invited the witness to repeat the last part of his answer, because I heard from the interpreters that they could not follow it. But I invited him to do it slowly. So therefore, I'm a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I was trying to just get to a response in answer to my question. But for the purposes of the record, we need to hear what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
