utterances.text: If you look at the page 87, line 237, that's what I was referring to. Mr. Mrksic, you said: "In other words to use our own forces, and relying on our own forces only, to force our politicians to proceed to a peaceful resolution of the issue in Croatia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that you added to this in your answer because that's where the interpreters lost you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I added this. It wasn't our goal to win in Croatia because realistically that was not possible, we just wanted to stabilize the front on the axis of Livno and Grahovo and on the Dinara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be able to proceed to this new option, not a wartime option, but rather a co-existence type of resolution, disarmament and so on, those who had leave Krajina, either if they had committed a crime or not, well, let them leave, and if not -- and to keep politicians in such a spot where they cannot trick people anymore but, rather, to proceed to serious negotiations with the Croatian government, because we could not expect any help from Serbia because they would not fight for anyone. Republika Srpska, in other words, took hands -- took things in their own hands, and they tried to resolve their own problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited you to repeat the last part of your question. I, however, get the impression that apart from repeating it, you added quite a bit. Perhaps if the future if I think you go too quickly, I will use my hand to give you signals to stop and take a breath and then to continue once you have taken that breath, and once it is indicated with my hand. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic, I'm going back to the line where you said you wanted the front lines to go back to where they were in mid-1994. To achieve that, you would have had to drive Croatian forces off of their positions in the Dinara and in the Grahovo area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: That was not realistically possible. The only possibility was to stabilize the front line. The plan was to start with special operations with Republika Srpska. However, this was just a decoy, because it was impossible to actually implement that plan. And when I realised that I was being lied to -- would you allow my to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I want to get to the question and draw your attention to your answer page 86, line 19, you said: "We would shift the front line and -- and this would return. In this way the situation in the Dinara would be reverted to where it was in 1994, mid-1994." My question to you is: Could you have reverted the front lines to where they were in mid-1994 without driving Croatian forces off the Dinara and out of Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: This was done before the Croatian forces entered Grahovo. They had not taken control over the entire Dinara. That's when we developed this plan, not once the Croatian forces entered Grahovo, because then it was a fait accompli. This should have been done earlier, in early July, instead of this Pauk [indiscernible] and so on, we should have done this part first and then Western Bosnia to stabilize the front line, rather than take control of, I don't know, 40 or 50 kilometres, but, rather, four to five kilometers. In other words to turn our backs on a military solution and move on to a political solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The translation now has finished. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Looking back at the document on the screen, General Mrksic, the last line on the page in English -- I'm not sure. I guess it should be the last line in the B/C/S. "General Mrksic is here, and as soon as" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "As soon as he left we made a decision to subordinate the Pauk command to him." Now, after this, was the Pauk command ultimately subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MRKSIC
utterances.text: During the operation, those 70 days or so, Mile Novakovic was issued assignment directly from me, not from the Republic of Serbia or from Fikret. I don't know who it was that he receive his tasks from. So it was from me, I was the commander, I commanded, and I issued orders for active operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The line that continues on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the -- there are technical problems with the French booth, although now listening to the French channel, I -- it seems that it has been resolved, or partly resolved only? Could I hear from the French booth? Yes. Everything is fine now from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm -- at the same time, I'm looking at the clock. Since we have been interrupted anyhow, I suggest that we would conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would first like the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Mrksic, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone, also not in the detention unit, with whomever, about your testimony, whether that is what you told us already today, or whether it is what you will still be asked about the days to come. But you should not speak with anyone about this. And we'd like to see you back. And we'll start tomorrow morning, 9.00. But we hope halfway the day that your counsel will arrive. We did our utmost best it resolve the matter. As you may understand, until now, there seems to be no major problem in terms of incriminating answers. This having said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just -- does the instruction include his counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instruction includes counsel. So even if there would be -- that means that if you would have telephone conversation, for example, with counsel, you are not allowed to speak about the questions and -- that were put to you, the answers given by you, you should not discuss it with anyone, not in the detention unit, not outside the detention unit, not by telephone, not by whatever technical means. Just don't -- do not speak with anyone about your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear. I am -- what I'm not clear on is how long will my testimony go on for, approximately, how many days? Because I had no conduct with anyone either with the Prosecutor or the Defence, and I don't know how long they intend to question me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The time the Defence asked for was nine hours, and then, of course, you may be cross-examined by the others, by the other parties, other Defence, Prosecution. So it will take quite a while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine hours. Does that mean five to six days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, three days examination-in-chief. But then have you to add perhaps similar time for cross-examination. That might take up quite a bit of time, Mr. Mrksic. I'm aware of that. Is there any reason why you are so concerned about it? No special programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. But next Wednesday, my daughter will be here, and my son-in-law, and I really do not wish to testify on that day, and I've written this to the gentleman. That's on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good that you tell us. We'll try to see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please try and wrap up by Tuesday, next Tuesday, to complete this on Tuesday. Tomorrow is what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might be too optimistic, as far as I can see now. Could you tell us this visit, family visit, is this planned for the morning or the afternoon, or for the whole of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the whole day, on the 24th, the 25th, and the 26th. So they arrive on Wednesday, the 24th. This was announced before I knew that I would be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we'll see to what extent we can accommodate you. I cannot promise you anything at this moment. One thing is for sure, that testimony will be given only either morning or afternoon. We will look into the matter, and we'll see what can be done, and if not, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if necessary, perhaps on one of these days, I can testify the whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could -- this is a suggestion. Of course, the Chamber might not be available for the whole of the day, but we will certainly consider any option which would accommodate you. And would you agree that we inquire with the detention unit when the visits exactly are scheduled so that we are able to the best of our abilities --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we will do that. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if perhaps we could ask the witness to take his earphones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the witness have to stay, because I already asked him to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do believe, depending on how the Court reacts to my comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have taken your earphones off. I do understand that the witness understands English very well. That's what Mr. Misetic said earlier, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Then perhaps I can make my comments outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has the witness to remain stand by for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Probably not, Your Honour. I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Mrksic, I've given you my instructions. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at -- yes. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, although we will not be in the same courtroom. We will be in Courtroom III. I will ask you to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will be very brief. My concern is that the Court's order to the witness not to speak to his lawyer about the testimony he has given or the testimony to be given, it escapes me how counsel is able to advise his client as to what questions or types of questions he would implicate his right against self-incrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that if counsel arrives tomorrow, we will have an opportunity to briefly address the matter with counsel. The witness will be present at that moment as well, and then we'll see to what extent we have to adapt the order. Now, I'll -- the Chamber will pay proper attention to that tomorrow. But I thought the instruction could not be clear enough today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So our position is clear, first, we don't see that the Prosecution has standing to raise the matter. Secondly, if it is for the witness to seek the advice of counsel, not for the lawyer to start talking -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss it at this moment in full detail. The think that the Chamber did its utmost best to keep everything in the appropriate order. And this certainly is a matter which we will -- and address in the presence of council what his role can be and cannot be, and how to communicate and, of course, if there's any specific matter then, of course, counsel could -- if there's any need, we could discuss this. I don't think it is an issue for which we should keep our interpreters and transcribers any further in court. We will adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, 18th of June, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24
